extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and graduate students (and instructors/researchers) studying algebraic topology; readers with standard undergraduate algebra and point-set topology background
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook exposition and reference for (classical) algebraic topology emphasizing CW complexes, homotopy, homology, and cohomology; suitable as a course text or self-study for readers with undergraduate algebra and point-set topology. Contains definitions, constructions, examples, optional additional topics, and appendices for technical point-set issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability and viewpoint priority
rubrics_metrics.description: This book was written to be a readable introduction to algebraic topology with rather broad coverage of the subject. The viewpoint is quite classical in spirit, and stays well within the confines of pure algebraic topology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readability is one of the first priorities of the book; exposition emphasizes geometric rather than algebraic aspects, avoiding 'wild innovation' while including a small number of mild novelties (e.g., use of complexes). Material is organized to favor intuition and accessibility over maximal generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites required
rubrics_metrics.description: The present book assumes the reader has some familiarity with the content of the standard undergraduate courses in algebra and point-set topology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular, the reader should know about quotient (identification) spaces. If not familiar, the preface lists recommended sources (e.g., Armstrong 1983, Jänich 1984).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and definition conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of mathematical terms are given within paragraphs of text, rather than displayed separately like theorems. These definitions are indicated by the use of boldface type for the more important terms, with italics being used for less important or less formal definitions as well as for simple emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms defined using boldface appear in the Index, with the page number where the definition occurs listed first. Readers should look for boldface/italics to identify formal vs informal definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention: continuity of maps
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid overusing the word ‘continuous’ we adopt the convention that maps between spaces are always assumed to be continuous unless otherwise stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: optional additional topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the four main chapters concludes with a selection of additional topics that the reader can sample at will, independent of the basic core of the book contained in the earlier parts of the chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These additional topics amount to nearly half the book; they are included to make the book more comprehensive and to give motivated readers substantial samples of deeper material. They can be skipped or read later as desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix usage policy
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an Appendix dealing mainly with a number of matters of a point-set topological nature that arise in algebraic topology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since this is a textbook on algebraic topology, details involving point-set topology are often treated lightly or skipped entirely in the body of the text; readers should consult the Appendix for those technicalities and for questions about point-set issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions / planned separate volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Not included in this book is the important but somewhat more sophisticated topic of spectral sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectral sequences are planned to be treated in a separate volume ('Spectral Sequences in Algebraic Topology'); other complementary volumes (e.g., vector bundles and K-theory) are also referenced for further topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of complexes (semisimplicial / Delta-complex) over simplicial complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: The book uses what are called 'complexes', a mild generalization of simplicial complexes that allows different faces of a simplex to coincide and drops the requirement that simplices are uniquely determined by their vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complexes are motivated as more efficient and pedagogically simpler for many examples (e.g., torus with 2 triangles instead of 14), are the natural domain for simplicial homology, and often arise from standard constructions. The choice is a deliberate expository convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cell complex (CW complex) construction requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A CW complex is constructed by (1) starting with a discrete set X^0 of 0-cells, (2) inductively forming X^n from X^{n-1} by attaching n-cells e^n_α via maps φ_α:S^{n-1}→X^{n-1}, and (3) giving the union the weak topology (if infinite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inductive process stops at finite n, X is finite-dimensional; skeletons X^n are subcomplexes; characteristic maps extend attaching maps and are homeomorphisms from the interior of D^n_α onto the cell. Use these structural rules when building or recognizing CW complexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcomplex and CW pair criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A subcomplex of a cell complex X is a closed subspace A⊂X that is a union of cells of X. A pair (X,A) with A a subcomplex is called a CW pair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because A is closed and a union of cells, characteristic maps and attaching maps of cells in A have images contained in A, so A itself is a cell complex. Skeletons X^n are primary examples of subcomplexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of CW complexes: cell structure and topology condition
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y are cell complexes, then X×Y has a CW structure with product cells e^m_α×e^n_β; however the CW topology on X×Y may be finer than the product topology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two topologies coincide if either X or Y has only finitely many cells, or if both X and Y have countably many cells. In practice the subtle point-set distinction rarely causes problems, but one should verify finiteness/countability hypotheses when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotient of a CW pair inherits CW structure
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X,A) is a CW pair, then the quotient space X/A inherits a natural cell complex structure. The cells of X/A are the cells of X−A together with a new 0-cell (the image of A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a cell e^n_α of X−A attached by φ_α:S^{n-1}→X^{n-1}, the attaching map in X/A is the composition S^{n-1}→X^{n-1}→X^{n-1}/A^{n-1}. Use this when reducing spaces to spheres or forming suspensions/quotients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension, join, wedge, and smash product CW-compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a CW complex then the suspension SX and cone CX are CW complexes (via quotient of X×I with product cell structure). More generally, the join X*Y, wedge X∨Y, and smash product X∧Y admit natural CW structures under the usual hypotheses on basepoints and cell structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For joins and smash products, if X and Y are CW complexes with chosen basepoints (0-cells) then X*Y and X∧Y are CW complexes with subcomplexes X and Y; be mindful of topology-vs-CW-topology issues analogous to product spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of deformation retraction and homotopy equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformation retraction of X onto A is a homotopy ft:X→X with f0=1, f1(X)=A, and ft|A=1 for all t. A map f:X→Y is a homotopy equivalence if there exists g:Y→X with fg≃1 and gf≃1; spaces X and Y then have the same homotopy type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deformation retractions are special homotopy equivalences; many concrete examples (mapping cylinder, cones) give deformation retractions. Use these notions to show spaces are contractible or have same homotopy type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collapsing subspaces as a criterion for homotopy equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Collapsing a subspace to a point usually has a drastic effect on homotopy type, but if the subspace being collapsed already has the homotopy type of a point, then collapsing it to a point might not change the homotopy type of the whole space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a practical method for constructing homotopy equivalences (collapse contractible subspaces). The text develops this idea (and a second method involving changing gluings) as commonly used techniques.
